description.summary: The Ahool is a reported giant bat- or flying-primate-like cryptid said to inhabit the rainforests and river valleys of western Java. It is best known from accounts gathered by the Dutch naturalist Ernest Bartels in the 1920s and popularised in English-language cryptozoology by Ivan T. Sanderson.
description.full: The Ahool is a cryptid reported from the mountainous rainforests of western Java, Indonesia. Its name is generally treated as onomatopoeic, imitating a drawn-out 'a-hooooool' cry that witnesses describe carrying through river valleys at night. The most-cited reports come from the Dutch-Indonesian naturalist Ernest Bartels, son of ornithologist M. E. G. Bartels: in 1925 Bartels reported being passed overhead by an enormous unknown flying creature near a waterfall on the Salak Mountains, and around 11:30 PM on a night in 1927 he heard the same loud 'a-hool' call from his hut near the Tjidjenkol River. Bartels' notes were taken up after his death by the cryptozoologist Ivan T. Sanderson, who promoted the Ahool in his 1948 article 'There Could Be Dinosaurs' and his 1967 book Living Mammals of the World as a candidate for an unknown giant bat or surviving primitive flying primate. Witness accounts give it a wingspan in the range of 3 to 3.7 m (10–12 ft), grey fur, a flattened, ape- or owl-like face, and clawed forelimbs; it is said to skim rivers at night to catch large fish. Mainstream zoologists generally explain the reports as misidentifications of large flying foxes (Pteropus vampyrus, the Indo-Malayan flying fox) or owls; no specimen, photograph, or remains has ever been produced.

etymology.origin: Sundanese / Indonesian; widely treated as onomatopoeic, imitating the creature's reported call.
etymology.meaning: Imitative of the long 'a-hool' cry attributed to it.
etymology.first_use: 1920s, in Ernest Bartels' field notes; popularised in English by Ivan T. Sanderson in the late 1940s and 1960s.

related_phenomena.name: Olitiau
related_phenomena.description: African giant-bat cryptid reported by Ivan T. Sanderson in Cameroon

related_phenomena.name: Orang-bati
related_phenomena.description: Indonesian flying humanoid cryptid from Seram

related_phenomena.name: Ropen
related_phenomena.description: Papua New Guinea flying cryptid reported as glowing and bat-like

features.description: Witness accounts give wingspans on the order of 3–3.7 m (10–12 ft); some popular accounts inflate this further.
Body covered in grey or dark grey fur in Bartels' accounts.
Described variously as ape-like, owl-like, or like a flattened monkey face with large dark eyes.
Large claws or hooks on the leading edge of the wings.

physical.morphology: A large nocturnal flying animal of disputed taxonomic affinity, variously interpreted as an outsized fruit bat or as a flying primate.

abilities.description: Strong, low, sustained flight along river corridors at night.
A long 'a-hool' cry from which the cryptid takes its name; reportedly audible at long distance through forested valleys.
Said to skim rivers at night to seize large fish.

habitat_preference: mountain caves and waterfalls of western Java
behavior.diet: Reported as piscivorous, taking fish from rivers; otherwise undescribed.
patterns: Active mostly at night near rivers
Reports cluster in the Salak and Halimun mountain regions of western Java

range.description: Reports are concentrated in the rainforests, river valleys, and volcanic uplands of western Java, particularly the Salak and Halimun mountain regions.

hotspots.name: Mount Salak

location.description: Volcanic mountain southwest of Bogor in West Java; site of Bartels' 1925 encounter near a waterfall

hotspots.notes: Bartels' first reported encounter occurred while exploring a waterfall in the Salak range.

hotspots.name: Tjidjenkol River area

location.description: River in western Java where Bartels reported a second encounter from his thatched hut around 11:30 PM

hotspots.notes: Spelling 'Tjidjenkol' reflects pre-1972 Dutch-era orthography of Sundanese rivers.

first_recorded.source: Ernest Bartels' field notes, as reported by Ivan T. Sanderson

peak_activity_periods.description: Bartels' encounters and contemporary Javanese reports
Sanderson's English-language articles and books bring the Ahool to Western cryptozoology

origins.cultural_roots: Sundanese folk tradition of large nocturnal flying creatures in the rainforests of western Java; absorbed into Western cryptozoology in the mid-20th century.
origins.earliest_accounts: Ernest Bartels' 1925 and 1927 encounters in the Salak mountains and Tjidjenkol river area, recorded in his unpublished field notes.
origins.folklore_connections: Linked by Sanderson to the Olitiau of Cameroon and to broader 'giant bat' traditions of equatorial forests.

timeline.event: Ernest Bartels reports being overflown by an enormous unknown flying creature while exploring a waterfall on Mount Salak in western Java
timeline.source: Bartels' field notes, summarised by Sanderson (1948, 1967)

timeline.event: Bartels reports a second Ahool encounter around 11:30 PM near the Tjidjenkol River in western Java
Ivan T. Sanderson publishes the Ahool reports in the article 'There Could Be Dinosaurs' in The Saturday Evening Post
timeline.significance: First English-language popular publication of Bartels' Ahool material
timeline.source: Sanderson, I. T. (1948), Saturday Evening Post

timeline.event: Sanderson includes the Ahool in his book Living Mammals of the World
timeline.significance: Standardises the cryptozoological framing of the Ahool as a possible giant bat
timeline.source: Sanderson, I. T. (1967), Living Mammals of the World

history.modern_era: The Ahool remains a frequently cited cryptid in popular cryptozoology and Indonesian travel writing. Mainstream biologists tend to attribute reports to the large flying fox Pteropus vampyrus, to large owls (especially the Javan eagle-owl Bubo sumatranus), or to misidentified herons; no specimen has ever been recovered.

notable.name: Bartels' 1925 Salak waterfall encounter

location.description: Waterfall on the slopes of the Salak Mountains, western Java

notable.description: While exploring a waterfall on the slopes of Mount Salak, Bartels reported being passed directly overhead by an enormous unknown bat- or primate-like flying creature.

factors: Account preserved primarily through later cryptozoological writing
credibility.notes: Foundational case for the Ahool tradition.

sources: Sanderson, I. T. (1948), 'There Could Be Dinosaurs', The Saturday Evening Post
Sanderson, I. T. (1967), Living Mammals of the World

notable.name: Bartels' 1927 Tjidjenkol River encounter

location.description: Bartels' thatched hut near the Tjidjenkol River, western Java

notable.description: Around 11:30 PM Bartels reported hearing the loud 'a-hool' cry pass over his hut, low above the river — the call from which the cryptid takes its name.

factors: Reported decades later by a third party

sources: Sanderson, I. T. (1967), Living Mammals of the World

documentary.name: Sanderson, 'There Could Be Dinosaurs'
documentary.description: Ivan T. Sanderson's article in The Saturday Evening Post that introduced Bartels' Ahool reports to a broad English-language audience.
documentary.analysis: Secondary account based on Bartels' notes; original primary documentation is sparse.
documentary.source: Sanderson, I. T. (1948), Saturday Evening Post

documentary.name: Sanderson, Living Mammals of the World
documentary.description: Sanderson's general zoology book containing his Ahool material.
documentary.source: Sanderson, I. T. (1967), Living Mammals of the World, Doubleday

scientific.name: Undescribed giant bat
scientific.description: Bartels and Sanderson interpreted the Ahool as a possible undescribed species of very large bat, taxonomically distinct from any known megabat.

scientific.name: Surviving primitive flying primate
scientific.description: An alternative cryptozoological hypothesis suggests the Ahool is not a bat at all but a relict population of an unknown gliding or flying primate, paralleling the Olitiau and other tropical flying-creature cryptids.
evidence_cited: Ape-like facial descriptions in some accounts

skeptical.name: Misidentified flying fox
skeptical.description: The Indo-Malayan flying fox (Pteropus vampyrus), the largest bat in the region, has a wingspan up to ~1.5 m and is plausibly enlarged in eyewitness memory. Most zoologists treat Ahool reports as misidentifications of this species.
evidence_cited: Distribution of Pteropus vampyrus across Java
Known difficulty of size estimation in low light

skeptical.name: Misidentified large owl
skeptical.description: The Javan eagle-owl (Bubo sumatranus) and other large owls produce loud calls and broad silhouettes at night and are sometimes invoked as more parsimonious explanations.
evidence_cited: Owl distribution and vocalisations in western Java forests

traditions: Sundanese forest traditions of large flying creatures along river valleys
stories: Bartels' 1925 and 1927 encounters as recounted by Sanderson
folklore.beliefs: The Ahool is treated locally as a real but rarely seen forest creature; in Western literature it is one of the standard 'tropical flying cryptids'.

literature: Ivan T. Sanderson — Living Mammals of the World (1967)
other: Frequent appearances in cryptozoology and mystery-animal television series

researchers.name: Ernest Bartels
researchers.contribution: Primary witness; recorded the Ahool encounters of 1925 and 1927 in his field notes

researchers.name: Ivan T. Sanderson
researchers.affiliation: Society for the Investigation of the Unexplained (SITU)
researchers.contribution: Brought the Ahool to English-language cryptozoology in 1948 and 1967

researchers.name: Karl Shuker
researchers.contribution: Modern cryptozoological commentary on the Ahool and the Olitiau

research.ongoing_studies: No active scientific field programme is investigating the Ahool; cryptozoological writing continues but produces no new primary evidence.
